reviews.reason: The solution set of a system is the intersection of each inequality's solution set. A student cannot find that intersection without first solving every single linear inequality correctly, including sign reversal.
After the constraints are modeled, the plans or parameter ranges are found from the system's common solution set. Determining integer plans depends on solving the system and taking the intersection.

reviews.scope: translating each verbal constraint into an inequality
reviews.reason: Listing a system means writing each condition, such as 'at most' or 'no less than', as an inequality. That translation and integer selection skill is the core of single-inequality applications.
The criterion asks students to compare plans using inequalities. Comparing two options usually needs one inequality, so multi-constraint system modeling enriches the project but is not necessary.
reviews.counterexample: Compare bus and car emissions by solving one inequality for the distance at which one plan is lower.

reviews.reason: Some emission relationships can be modeled with two unknowns, so prior word-problem modeling with systems helps. The inequality comparison criterion itself does not depend on it.
reviews.counterexample: Model each plan's emissions with one-variable expressions and compare them directly.

reviews.reason: Distinguishing a census from a sample survey concerns who is surveyed and why. It does not use two-way table reading or row and column totals. A better prerequisite is the statistical investigation process.
reviews.counterexample: A student who has never read a two-way table can still decide that testing light bulb lifetimes requires sampling.

reviews.scope: identifying the sample as surveyed subset
reviews.reason: A sample and its size only make sense as the part of the population actually surveyed in a sampling survey. Identifying them presupposes understanding sampling as investigating part of the whole.

reviews.scope: judging whether a sample reflects the population
reviews.reason: Representativeness is a relation between a sample and its population. Spotting biased sampling requires identifying the population and recognizing which individuals the sample omits.

reviews.scope: line chart part of chart choice
reviews.reason: The middle-school node itself teaches what line charts show and how to read trends. Elementary line-graph experience is a helpful review, but the later node subsumes it.
reviews.counterexample: A student taught line, bar and pie charts together in this lesson can choose a line chart for trends.

reviews.scope: pie chart part of chart choice
reviews.reason: Reading proportions from a pie chart is explicitly taught within this node's comparison of chart types. Prior elementary pie charts help with review, but they are not a necessary separate stage.
reviews.counterexample: Learn sector charts as part-of-whole displays directly while comparing the three chart types.

reviews.reason: A frequency distribution table is essentially a one-way table of group counts. Experience reading cells and totaling columns helps, but the two-category structure of two-way tables is not needed.
reviews.counterexample: Tally raw data into class intervals and record counts without ever using a two-way table.

reviews.reason: Choosing a class width, the number of groups, and tallying are tabulation skills. They do not build on selecting or reading pie, bar or line charts.
reviews.counterexample: Complete a frequency table from raw height data before any chart is introduced.

reviews.reason: Each histogram bar represents the frequency of one class interval. Drawing or interpreting histograms therefore depends on grouping data into intervals and counting frequencies per group.
Histograms use horizontal and vertical scales like bar charts. They do not need ordered-pair coordinates, negative quadrants or plotting points, so the coordinate plane is only loosely associated.
reviews.counterexample: Draw a histogram on grid paper using bar chart scaling experience only.

reviews.reason: Trend charts are line-type displays, so line chart reading helps. Elementary line graphs already supply that skill, and choosing among the three chart types is not needed.
reviews.counterexample: A student with elementary line-graph knowledge can describe a rising trend and extrapolate.

reviews.reason: Daylight versus date is time-series data, so trend charts fit naturally. An ordinary line chart, or even a table, can still reveal and describe the seasonal pattern.
reviews.counterexample: Plot daylight hours on a basic line graph and describe seasonal rise and fall.

reviews.reason: Histograms display distributions and are not suited to showing change over time. They are at most an optional tool for comparing locations, not a helpful preparation for the project.
reviews.counterexample: Complete the investigation with tables and line graphs only.

reviews.reason: The project follows the cycle of questioning, collecting, organizing and describing data. Knowing that process helps structure it, though students can carry it out with guidance without naming the steps.
reviews.counterexample: Follow a teacher worksheet step by step without explicitly knowing the formal process stages.

reviews.scope: classifying triangles by sides and angles
reviews.reason: This node reteaches and extends classification by both sides and angles, including the scalene category. Elementary classification is a helpful review, but the later node subsumes it.
reviews.counterexample: Learn acute, right, obtuse, isosceles and equilateral classifications freshly in this lesson.

reviews.scope: sides as line segments with endpoints
reviews.reason: A triangle is defined as three segments joined end to end, and sides are named by their endpoint vertices. Recognizing segments and their notation is needed to identify the basic elements.

reviews.scope: applying side inequalities to triangle sides
reviews.reason: The inequalities concern the three sides of a triangle. Judging whether three segments can form a triangle presupposes knowing what a triangle and its sides are.
The shortest-segment fact explains why two sides exceed the third. The criteria only require applying the inequality to test lengths and find ranges, which can be learned from experiments.
reviews.counterexample: Discover the rule by trying to form triangles with sticks of different lengths, then apply it.

reviews.scope: ranges when side lengths are algebraic
reviews.reason: With numeric sides, the range a minus b to a plus b needs only arithmetic. Solving linear inequalities helps only when side lengths involve unknowns, such as x plus 1.
reviews.counterexample: Given sides 3 and 5, state 2 < c < 8 by subtraction and addition.

reviews.scope: vertex and opposite side for altitudes
reviews.reason: An altitude is defined from a vertex to the opposite side or its extension. Identifying these elements, and recognizing acute, right and obtuse cases, depends on the triangle concept.

reviews.scope: altitude as perpendicular segment and construction
reviews.reason: An altitude is the perpendicular segment from a vertex. Drawing it, especially outside an obtuse triangle, uses the set-square method for drawing a perpendicular through a point to a line.

reviews.scope: vertex and opposite side for medians
reviews.reason: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Its area-bisecting property also refers to triangle area, so the triangle elements must be understood first.

reviews.scope: locating the midpoint of the opposite side
reviews.reason: Constructing a median requires finding the midpoint of the opposite side. The equal-area argument also uses the two equal half-bases created by that midpoint.
A triangle's angle bisector segment runs from a vertex to the opposite side. Recognizing the interior angles and the opposite sides requires the triangle concept.
The triangle angle bisector is defined by splitting an interior angle into two equal parts. Knowing what an angle bisector is and how to draw one comes from the general angle work.
The theorem relates the three interior angles of a triangle. Finding an unknown angle requires identifying those angles and their vertices in the figure.

The criterion asks students to explain the proof. Euclidean proofs of the angle sum rely on alternate or corresponding angles from a parallel line, since the theorem depends on the parallel postulate.
Both the property and its converse follow by subtracting 90 degrees from the 180 degree sum. The angle sum is the essential justification for each direction.
The exterior angle property can be proved directly with a parallel line through the vertex, or used computationally once stated. The angle sum is the customary but not unique route.
reviews.counterexample: Draw a line through C parallel to AB; corresponding and alternate angles show the exterior angle equals A plus B.

reviews.reason: Writing 'given' and 'to prove' means splitting a proposition into its condition and conclusion. Citing a reason for each step relies on knowing definitions, axioms and theorems.
The angle sum proof is a convenient worked example of the given, to-prove, proof format. Any other simple theorem, such as vertical angles being equal, could serve instead.
reviews.counterexample: Learn the proof format using the vertical-angles theorem.

reviews.scope: centroid as the intersection of medians
reviews.reason: The criterion asks students to explain that a triangle's centre of gravity is the medians' intersection. That explanation needs the median concept and the fact that the three medians meet.

reviews.scope: intuition that moving preserves shape and size
reviews.reason: Congruence is defined by complete superposition. Translation offers one intuition for shape-preserving motion, but rotation, reflection or physically overlaying cutouts work equally well.
reviews.counterexample: Cut out two triangles and check by stacking that they coincide.

reviews.reason: Identifying corresponding elements and writing the congruence statement needs the triangle's vertices, sides and angles. Without these elements, correspondence cannot be stated.
A translated figure coincides with the original, which gives a concrete example of congruence. Superposition can also be understood without formal translation properties.
reviews.counterexample: Define congruence by overlaying traced figures without studying translation.

reviews.reason: The properties state that corresponding parts are equal. Applying them requires the congruence definition and correct matching of corresponding vertices in the notation.

reviews.scope: motivating SSS as a converse criterion
reviews.reason: Proving triangles congruent by SSS needs the congruence definition and correspondence. The properties motivate why the criterion matters and support later conclusions, but are not needed to state or apply SSS.
reviews.counterexample: Prove triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF by SSS, with no follow-up angle conclusion.

reviews.reason: SSS compares two existing triangles with equal sides. The triangle inequality only matters when constructing a triangle from arbitrary lengths, which is not part of the criteria.
reviews.counterexample: Apply SSS to two given triangles without considering whether arbitrary lengths form a triangle.

reviews.reason: Identifying the included angle and proving congruence by SAS rely on the congruence definition. The properties motivate the criterion and support later conclusions, but are not needed for SAS itself.
reviews.counterexample: Prove two triangles congruent by SAS and stop at the congruence statement.

reviews.reason: Exploring SAS repeats the SSS investigation of which minimal conditions fix a triangle. The analogy helps, but SAS can be stated and used independently.
reviews.counterexample: Learn SAS first through compass and ruler construction.

reviews.reason: Stating ASA and AAS and proving congruence with them require the congruence definition. The properties help motivate the criteria but are not logically required for them.
reviews.counterexample: Use ASA to establish a congruence without deriving any equal parts afterward.

reviews.reason: The criterion explicitly requires deriving AAS from ASA. That step uses the angle sum to show the third angles are equal, turning AAS into ASA.
Stating HL and recognizing when to use it rely on congruence and correspondence. The properties of congruent triangles motivate the criterion but are not logically needed to apply HL.
reviews.counterexample: Prove two right triangles congruent by HL without deducing further equal parts.

reviews.scope: right triangle as object of HL
reviews.reason: HL needs the right triangle concept and the terms hypotenuse and leg, not the complementarity of the acute angles. A better prerequisite is triangle concept and classification.
reviews.counterexample: Apply HL knowing only which side is the hypotenuse, without using complementary acute angles.

reviews.reason: HL can be explained through SSS after finding the third side, and judging when only HL applies requires contrasting it with other criteria. Construction offers an alternative justification.
reviews.counterexample: Justify HL by construction: a right angle, a leg, then an arc for the hypotenuse gives a unique triangle.

reviews.scope: selecting SSS when three sides are known
reviews.reason: Choosing a criterion requires knowing every available option. When only sides are known, SSS is the applicable criterion, so selection is impossible without it.

reviews.scope: selecting SAS and supplying missing conditions
reviews.reason: Combined problems often require recognizing two sides with their included angle, or adding a condition to complete SAS. Proper selection requires mastery of SAS.

reviews.scope: selecting ASA or AAS from angle data
reviews.reason: When the givens are mainly angles plus one side, the student must decide between ASA and AAS. Choosing among all criteria requires mastering these two.
Some right triangle cases fit only HL, since side, side, non-included angle fails in general. Correct method selection therefore requires knowing HL and when it applies.
The criterion requires complete, properly written proofs. That needs the given, to-prove, proof structure with a cited reason for every step.
